newsitem.title: GERMANY: German local TV station declares bankruptcy.
newsitem.headline: German local TV station declares bankruptcy.

text.p: German television station Puls-TV said on Wednesday it had declared bankruptcy, two weeks after its investors pulled funding on the ailing channel.

But the small regional network that has focused on Berlin and the surrounding state of Brandenburg and was formerly known as 1A said it would continue broadcasting reruns of programming as long as possible.
"After the investors of Puls-TV discontinued funding of the station, the management of the private regional station sees itself forced to declare bankruptcy," the channel said in a statement.
"All attempts by the management to achieve further financing for the channel have remained unsuccessful."
A spokeswoman for the private station, which serves Berlin and surrounding Brandenburg, said it will broadcast reruns for as long as possible while a local court processes its bankruptcy claim.

Central European Media Enterprises (CME), a U.S. company with investments in private television throughout central and eastern Europe, announced two weeks ago it would stop financing the station and was taking a $20 million writedown against its German operations.
It said at the time the development of the Berlin television advertising market had been disappointing.

CME had been the only partner still funding the station during the 18 months it was posting losses of about two million marks a month. Other investors included Time Warner Entertainment and investor George Soros.

The network was founded in 1993 and owners had invested about 130 million marks in it. But it struggled in the ratings, never able to garner more than a one percent market share in Germany's competitive television market.
Puls TV has 130 employees and uses the services of about 70 freelance journalists.
